How the story of my feet changed

The original notes, what was typed afterwards, and what happened over the following years.

The story in a few minutes

In 2017, I went into hospital with worsening movement, balance, stiffness and foot problems. The GP had noticed that my unusual walking, tense muscles, clawing toes and painful feet were happening together.

During the hospital interview, I explained that after leaving bar work in 2012, the pain in my feet had become less prominent. That made me more aware of the tension in my legs. The handwritten note records that I had begun to notice the two were different.

When the history was typed up, that became a statement that I had realised they were not the same problem. The neurologist's impression went further, describing me as having “markedly divorced” the tension from the foot pain in my own mind, while suggesting that the painful feet might have a separate cause, possibly peripheral neuropathy.

At the same admission, the neurologist had observed a left-leg movement that looked possibly dystonic and treated my leg tension with clonazepam. That does not prove the foot lesions were caused by the movement disorder. It does raise an obvious question: what showed that the pain in my feet was separate from the movement and tension problems?

Over the following years, foot symptoms were repeatedly described alongside abnormal movement or changes in Parkinson's medication. That made the original separation worth examining again.

How the wording changed

Most of the early typed history follows the handwriting closely. The important change happens around the sentence about leaving bar work and noticing foot pain and leg tension separately.

Handwritten interviewTyped accountWhy it matters
“for the most part I took pain in my feet out of [the] picture”Foot pain had improved “to a degree” after leaving bar work.The typed account adds a qualification and makes the link to work more explicit. CLIN-000971–973
“Began to be aware”“began to realise”Noticing a difference is expressed more like reaching a conclusion. CLIN-000974–976
“foot pain & leg tension weren’t the same”“were not the same problem” — with “Therefore” and “because”Two different experiences become two distinct “problems” in the telling. CLIN-000974–976
No equivalent wording on the three handwritten pages“markedly divorced” the two “in his own mind”The impression attributes a much stronger separation to the patient. CLIN-001146–149
No equivalent diagnosis on the three handwritten pagesFoot symptoms “may” be separate, “perhaps” peripheral neuropathy, possibly linked to alcohol; “Not clear.”A possible medical explanation is added, but explicitly remains uncertain. CLIN-001142–145

These are comparisons of written records. The original handwritten notes were made by the neurologist during the interview; they are not a full verbatim recording of everything said.

What the neurologist saw and treated

On examination, the walking was described as “strikingly abnormal”. The left leg made a movement like foot drop, but the note said it was possibly a dystonic posture, “NOT FOOT DROP”. The examination also recorded gross slowness of movement, flat arches and hammertoes. CLIN-001085–132

“Clonazepam was given at night to relieve tension in the legs.”

Clonazepam appears in the discharge record at 0.25 mg at night. The treatment plan also considered replacing it with nighttime procyclidine if tolerated. CLIN-001182–188; CLIN-001651–653; CLIN-001694–704

So the neurologist was already observing abnormal lower-limb movement and treating leg tension. The question is not whether neuropathy was impossible. It is why some of the painful foot symptoms were put into a potentially separate explanation, and what examination or other information supported that division. CLIN-001142–149

What happened afterwards

2017–2018: After a period without procyclidine, worsening tension and movement were reported alongside a rapid return of a problem described as an outside-left-foot corn. The later note described that same withdrawal episode; it is not a second experiment. CLIN-001770–790; CLIN-001914–918

2019: A GP podiatry referral explicitly connected earlier foot problems with increased tone and an abnormal Parkinsonian gait, and described clawing feet and pain. CLIN-003091–107

2020: Neurology examined another footdrop-like movement and called it “actually parkinsonian” after finding normal ankle movement strength. CLIN-002284–288

2023–2025: Severe foot and leg pain continued. Some notes linked pain and shuffling to medication OFF periods; the 2025 record said foot symptoms eased when Parkinson's medication took effect, while neuropathy was still discussed as a possibility. CLIN-002574–583; CLIN-002633–641; CLIN-002768–800

None of these observations proves one cause for every foot symptom. Together, they explain why the earlier division between pain and movement remained an important question.

6. Documentary progression — July 2017 and later

3 July 2017 — handwritten history

“Began to be aware that foot pain & leg tension weren’t the same…” — a reported distinction in experience.

July 2017 — typed history

“Began to realise” / “not the same problem” / “Therefore” / “because” — a stronger interpretive formulation (CLIN-000974–976).

July 2017 — final impression

Possible separate peripheral neuropathy and alcohol association, alongside “markedly divorced” as an attribution to the patient (CLIN-001142–149).

2018–2025 — follow-up

Medication-state observations, foot phenomena, abnormal movement, gait and pain raise questions about how the early division was reconsidered; they do not establish a common cause.

The order above represents the manuscript’s documentary comparison, not proven drafting/transcription chronology, causal influence, deliberate alteration or authorship. Native clinical documents and metadata control any disputed provenance.

Detailed neurological finding, treatment and foot-pain comparison

Audit finding — observed left-lower-limb abnormality, treatment of leg tension, and the proposed foot-pain partition

Scope and status: This is an evidence-anchored audit formulation derived from The Three Pages and the Nine-Year Record, read together with the handwritten interview and supplied CLIN images. CLIN references are retrieval anchors; original examination, treatment, and signed discharge records control exact wording. This is an assessment of documentary reasoning, not a diagnosis or a finding of misconduct.

Audit formulation

In July 2017, Neurology documented a dystonic-looking left lower-limb abnormality and undertook pharmacological treatment of leg tension. Against that contemporaneous evidence, the subsequent separation of painful foot symptoms into a possible peripheral-neuropathy explanation required an identifiable clinical rationale. The available handwritten history did not itself establish pathological independence, and the final impression expressly acknowledged uncertainty. The documentary question is what positive evidence justified the partition and how the existing neurological findings were reconciled with it.

“Subsequent” refers to the progression of the clinical narrative from history and examination/treatment to impression, not a verified timestamp order of writing, dictation or signature.

Evidence linked to the formulation

Audit question and limits

Question for the clinical record: What examination, sensory findings, neurophysiology, further patient history or explicit comparison of dystonic/postural, mechanical and neuropathic mechanisms justified treating the painful feet as sufficiently separate from the observed and treated neurological lower-limb presentation? Where was that reasoning documented, and when was it revisited after later treatment-state evidence?

Limits: Distinct sensations need not mean separate diseases; equally, an abnormal gait and treatment for leg tension do not prove that corns, calluses or burning were caused by dystonia or Parkinsonism. Peripheral neuropathy could coexist. No inference of intentional alteration is made. The reviewed extracts do not establish that every relevant assessment was absent from the complete medical record.

The original source images are embedded in this file, so it can be read offline. The medical questions remain open where the records do not settle them.
